title: Alekhine Defense: Four Pawns Attack
subtitle: How far can a center expand before it breaks?
summary: White accepts every invitation Black offers and builds the most ambitious possible center — four connected pawns on c4, d4, e5, and f4. It is the most direct answer to the whole premise of Alekhine's Defense: rather than trading down or developing modestly, White simply keeps advancing and asks Black to prove the center really is overextended. Sharp, double-edged, and one of the deepest independent bodies of theory the opening produces.

metadata.historicalContext: White's most theoretically ambitious reply to Alekhine's Defense — a large, sharply analyzed body of independent theory distinct from the calmer 4.Nf3 main lines.

rootAnnotations.title: What this lesson teaches
rootAnnotations.body: The family study asked whether a big White center is a strength or a target; the Exchange Variation answered by trading it down early. The Four Pawns Attack answers the opposite way — build the biggest center legally possible and defend it with pieces. Four connected pawns control an enormous amount of space, but every pawn move is also a move that isn't developing a piece, and the pawns themselves can become targets the moment Black finds the right lever against them. Watch for the recurring question: is this center a wall, or a house of cards?

annotations.title: The maximal try
annotations.body: White now controls c4, d4, e5, and f4 — a genuine four-pawn wall stretching across the board. It's an enormous space advantage, but notice what's missing: no White piece besides the knight on f3-to-be has developed yet, and the king is still on e1. This is the tradeoff in miniature — maximum space today, for development and structural commitments that Black gets to target for the rest of the game.

Black challenges the front pawn immediately, matching the family study's recurring theme: don't let the tension sit unresolved. Two White pawns could recapture here — which one, and why does it matter?

annotations.title: The recapture that keeps the center intact
annotations.body: Recapturing with the f-pawn keeps d4 covered by a pawn and opens the f-file for White's rook, useful for the kingside play this variation is built around. Recapturing with the d-pawn instead is playable, but it leaves d4 without a pawn defender for the rest of the game — a square Black's pieces would be glad to use later. Either way, d5 itself stays controlled by the c4 pawn — see the variation here for the idea.

annotations.title: The other recapture
annotations.body: Keeping a pawn on f4 instead of d4 aims the structure differently, but it leaves d4 without a pawn defender for the rest of the game — one reason fxe5 remains the far more common choice.
A second piece joins the pressure against d4 and e5 — the same piece-pressure idea from the family study, now aimed at a bigger, more extended target.
White adds a defender to d4 and prepares further development. Simple and necessary — the center needs support, not just pawns.

annotations.title: Solving the problem bishop early
annotations.body: In cramped structures like this one, Black's light-squared bishop is normally the piece that suffers — it can easily get shut in behind its own pawns once ...e6 is played. Getting it out to f5 before closing the center with ...e6 is a small but genuinely transferable idea: whenever your position is about to become cramped, ask which piece will be trapped by your own pawns, and move it first.
White's last minor piece develops. Note the diagonal this opens for Black — a pin on this knight is now available if Black wants it, as the variation on Black's next move shows.

annotations.title: Preparing to castle long
annotations.body: The queen steps aside for queenside castling and connects the rooks. Black could instead pin the newly developed knight immediately — a genuine independent try shown in the variation here.

annotations.title: The pin instead of the plan
annotations.body: Rather than preparing to castle, Black pins the f3 knight to the queen on d1, adding indirect pressure to the center before committing the king anywhere.

annotations.title: The race begins
annotations.body: Black castles queenside, away from White's slightly overextended kingside pawns. When White castles short next move, the position becomes an opposite-side-castling race — an inversion of the usual roles, since it's White's own extended center that will need to be turned into a kingside attack while Black's pieces aim back at it.

annotations.title: The four-pawn center, fully committed
annotations.body: Both kings have chosen sides, and the whole game now hinges on whose attack arrives first. White's plans run through the extra central space — a further d5 break, or simply more pieces joining the kingside; Black's plans run through undermining the pawn chain directly, classically with a timely ...f6 or ...c5, or a straightforward kingside pawn storm now that the target is White's own king rather than Black's.

annotations.title: What you should have noticed
annotations.body: Three lessons to carry forward: a maximal center is a real strength, not a bluff — White genuinely controls more space here than in any other Alekhine's Defense line — but every pawn spent building it is a piece not yet developed, which is exactly why Black's pressure (Nc6, Bf5, the ...Bg4 pin) all arrived so quickly; solving your worst-placed piece before the position closes (Bf5 before e6) is a transferable habit, not a one-off trick; and opposite-side castling races reward whoever converts space into a direct attack first — space alone is not enough. Compare this maximal approach with the Exchange Variation's calmer answer to the same central question.
